history.heading: Polynesian origins
paragraphs: The Samoan Islands were settled around 3,000 years ago by people of the Lapita culture, ancestors of the Polynesians. Samoa is often considered a cradle of Polynesian culture, from which settlers later voyaged to other islands.
Samoan society developed around extended families (aiga) led by chiefs (matai), and the islands had close ties with Tonga and Fiji.

history.heading: Colonial division
paragraphs: European contact began in the 18th century, and missionaries arrived in 1830, converting most Samoans to Christianity. Rivalry between Germany, the United States and Britain over the islands led to the Tripartite Convention of 1899, which divided Samoa.

The eastern islands, including Tutuila with its deep harbour at Pago Pago, went to the United States, which used Pago Pago as a naval coaling station. Local chiefs ceded the islands in 1900 and 1904, and Swains Island was added in 1925.

history.heading: Modern era
paragraphs: The US Navy administered the territory until 1951, when responsibility passed to the Department of the Interior. American Samoa adopted its own constitution in 1967 and has elected its own governor since 1977.
In 2009 an earthquake and tsunami caused deaths and severe damage, especially on Tutuila.

culture.heading: Fa'a Samoa
paragraphs: Life follows fa'a Samoa, the Samoan way, which emphasises family, respect for elders and chiefs, church and communal sharing. Most land is communally owned by extended families and cannot easily be sold to outsiders.
Samoan and English are both official, and most people are bilingual. Christianity is central to community life, with Sunday church services and choirs very important.

culture.heading: Arts and sport
paragraphs: Traditional arts include tatau (tattooing), from which the English word "tattoo" comes, siva dancing and fire-knife dancing. Food often comes from an umu, an earth oven of hot stones.
American Samoa is famous for producing a remarkable number of American football players relative to its small population.

politics.heading: Status
paragraphs: American Samoa is an unincorporated, unorganised territory of the United States. People born there are US nationals rather than US citizens by birth, an issue that has been debated in the courts, and they cannot vote in US presidential elections.

The territory elects a governor and lieutenant governor and has a legislature called the Fono, whose Senate is chosen by county councils according to Samoan custom. It sends one non-voting delegate to the US House of Representatives.

economy.heading: Tuna and government
paragraphs: The economy depends heavily on tuna canning and on the territorial government, which is funded largely by US federal grants. The cannery in Pago Pago has been one of the largest private employers, and canned tuna dominates exports, mostly to the United States.
Tourism is limited by remoteness. The National Park of American Samoa protects rainforests and coral reefs. The currency is the US dollar, and many people move to Hawaii or the US mainland for work.
